## 4. Remaining exact gap

The reduction above removes rollable ghosts after selecting a diameter-preserving local plateau representative. It does not show that trapped ghosts themselves can be removed.

A genuine positive construction still requires exact coordinates with all pair inequalities verified, forest FFF, the appropriate stress certificate, and an ordinary-local proof accounting for every weakly active constraint. First-order KKT conditions alone are insufficient.

Conversely, a nonexistence theorem would need to show that every forest candidate with the necessary trapped ghosts nevertheless admits a coupled feasible shortening motion. Neither the rolling argument nor the numerical test establishes that.

There is also no implication from this finite/local question to the eventual-global Erdős assertion without an additional argument.

# Positive-stress block strategy: a rigorous anchor-and-separator theorem

Result: Every cyclic block of the positive-contact graph requires at least three noncollinear anchors (loaded diameter endpoints or attachment vertices). Moreover, a component separated by a cutvertex and containing exactly one loaded endpoint is necessarily a straight unit path.

These conclusions use only equilibrium, positive contact weights and unit separation. They do not require the conditional assertion that every loaded vertex is a nonarticulation.

They yield an exact block-counting identity and a useful diameter-force condition on every positive bridge. They do not establish O(D)O(D)O(D) total cyclic edges or exclude two cyclic blocks.

## 1. Setup

Let P⊂R2P\subset\mathbb R^2P⊂R2 be finite, unit-separated, with diameter D>1D>1D>1. Distinguish:

- FFF: all actual unit contacts;
- HHH: all actual diameter endpoints;
- T⊆FT\subseteq FT⊆F: edges with strictly positive contact multiplier;

Conclusion: Not for local minimax optimality under MFCQ, LICQ, or even the usual second-order sufficient condition on the original critical cone. This distinction is important for the full-contact-forest obstruction. The universal ghost-endpoint theorem does not, by itself, yield a diameter-decreasing deformation.

## 1. Primary tensegrity results

Robert Connelly and Walter Whiteley, Second-Order Rigidity and Prestress Stability for Tensegrity Frameworks, SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics 9 (1996), 453–491.

[Author-hosted full PDF](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~connelly/pdf/10.1137_S0895480192229236.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) · [Journal DOI](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0895480192229236?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Three results are directly relevant.

Theorem 2.3.2, p. 459 — first-order stress test. A specified cable can be shortened, or strut lengthened, strictly to first order by an admissible infinitesimal flex if and only if its coefficient vanishes in every proper self-stress.

This confirms the significance of universal zero support, rather than zero in one chosen stress. It does not prove that the infinitesimal flex integrates into a finite motion. pi.math.cornell.edu

Corollary 5.2.1, p. 479 — second-order stress test. A given first-order flex vvv extends to a second-order flex precisely when

vTΩ(ω)v≤0v^{T}\Omega(\omega)v\leq 0vTΩ(ω)v≤0

Proposition 3.3.2 and Remark 3.3.1, pp. 463–464. Prestress stability implies rigidity. The authors permit unstressed unilateral members to be deleted when constructing a prestress-stability certificate, but do not assert that deleting them preserves rigidity or local optimization. They expressly exclude stiffness contributions from unstressed cables and struts in that certificate. pi.math.cornell.edu

Connelly–Whiteley, Figure 9(b), p. 467, provides a particularly relevant geometric warning.

Their planar tensegrity has unstressed connecting members, including a short horizontal cable and a horizontal strut. The framework is rigid, but deleting those members destroys rigidity. Remark 4.4.1 further identifies the original framework as second-order rigid without being prestress stable.

Thus unstressed unilateral members can be indispensable to the nonlinear feasible geometry. This is a genuine Euclidean cable–strut example, not an example of a globally optimal unit-separated packing or an MFCQ-qualified diameter minimax problem. pi.math.cornell.edu

Every proper self-stress of G−WG-WG−W extends by zero on WWW to a proper self-stress of GGG.

Conversely, every proper self-stress of GGG is already supported on G−WG-WG−W, by hypothesis.

Consequently, the proper self-stress cones of the two frameworks are identical under zero extension. Their quadratic stress tests on vvv are therefore identical.

Applying Connelly–Whiteley Corollary 5.2.1 proves the equivalence. □\square□

## 2. Geleji–Jordán: closest structural predecessor

János Geleji and Tibor Jordán, Robust Tensegrity Polygons, EGRES Technical Report TR-2012-15 (2012), published in Discrete & Computational Geometry 50, 537–551 (2013).

Primary sources: [authorial preprint](https://egres.elte.hu/tr/egres-12-15.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [published article DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-013-9539-4?utm_source=chatgpt.com). egres.elte.hu+1

The preprint's Lemma 2.5 states:

> Let TTT be a strong abstract tensegrity polygon with two strut components. Suppose that vvv is a cut-vertex in one of the strut components. Then vvv is strut-covered.

Here strut-covered means that a strut connects the two neighbors of vvv along the polygon's boundary cable cycle.

Its proof invokes:

- Lemma 2.3: deleting a vertex that is not strut-covered and replacing its two incident boundary cables by one cable preserves strongness.
- Lemma 2.4: a tensegrity polygon with at least three strut components cannot be strong.

Consequently, deleting a noncovered cut-vertex would produce at least three strut components while preserving strongness, a contradiction. egres.elte.hu+1

Precise corollary: In a strong abstract tensegrity polygon with exactly two strut components, a vertex that is not strut-covered cannot be an articulation vertex of a strut component.

That is a genuine conditional nonarticulation theorem. But there are four critical hypothesis differences.

First, a tensegrity polygon has all vertices strictly convex, with its cables forming the entire convex boundary Hamiltonian cycle. Positive unit contacts in the present packing generally form an interior network, not such a cycle.

Second, strong means every convex realization has a nontrivial proper equilibrium stress. Our assertion requires one specific geometric realization with one nonnegative physical equilibrium certificate.

Third, with the natural stress-sign assignment, unit edges are cables and diameter edges are struts. Geleji–Jordán's strut components therefore do not represent our contact graph TTT. Simultaneously reversing cable and strut labels does not supply the missing convex Hamiltonian boundary structure.

Fourth, triangle-freeness of the full unit graph forbids edges between two unit neighbors of a vertex. It does not automatically forbid a strut between the two boundary cable neighbors in Geleji–Jordán's model.

Thus Lemma 2.5 becomes applicable only after substantial extra reductions establishing its special polygonal hypotheses and the required noncoverage. Those reductions are not consequences of the cited lemma.

## 3. Connelly–Whiteley: precise stress-duality predecessor

Robert Connelly and Walter Whiteley, Second-Order Rigidity and Prestress Stability for Tensegrity Frameworks, SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics 9 (1996), 453–491.

Primary: [author-hosted published paper](https://connellytensegrity.com/pdf/10.1137_S0895480192229236.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [journal DOI](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0895480192229236?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

Theorem 2.3.2, the first-order stress test, says that a prescribed cable or strut can change length strictly in an admissible first-order flex exactly when every proper self-stress vanishes on that member. The paper attributes this test to an earlier Whiteley manuscript, reference [35]. This matters for historical attribution: the accessible 1996 published statement is not presented by its authors as an entirely new duality principle. connellytensegrity.com+1

The theorem applies to arbitrary finite tensegrities, so its algebraic scope covers the unit-contact/diameter framework. It does not, however, imply the loaded-articulation conclusion merely from connectivity or triangle-freeness.

In particular, producing virtual rotations is not enough to apply the theorem as a feasible-flex statement unless all cable and strut first-order inequalities are checked. The more direct route here uses virtual velocities exclusively in the equilibrium identity. That argument needs no assertion that the velocities are globally feasible or integrable.

This construction supplies a definite answer to the assigned affine-deformation question:

- Balanced positive- and negative-slope diameter constraints can occur at exact rational parameters strictly below 1/21/21/2, arbitrarily close to 1/21/21/2.

Even globally optimal affine lattice shapes, with exactly balanced diametral constraints and asymptotically optimal density, need not provide evidence of unrestricted global optimality. ## 2. Precise hypotheses and the train-track crossing lemma

The proof needs the following interpretation of the tiling condition.

The polygon KKK has nonempty interior. Its tiles are genuine nondegenerate rhombi of side length exactly one, with pairwise disjoint interiors, meeting only along full shared edges or at vertices. Collinear subdivision vertices along the boundary are allowed. Holes and nonconvex patches are not.

### Lemma: Every pair of distinct edge directions occurs together in a rhombus

This claim is valid for convex edge-to-edge rhombus tilings.

Proof. Fix an unoriented edge direction uuu. A train track is formed by entering a rhombus across a uuu-parallel edge and leaving through its opposite uuu-parallel edge, repeatedly.

Within each rhombus the track crosses the strip between those parallel edges. Its displacement has a strictly positive component in a consistently chosen normal direction to uuu. Thus the track progresses monotonically in that normal coordinate.

It cannot close into a cycle or terminate inside the tiling. Since the tiling is finite, every track has two boundary endpoints.

Now consider the boundary edges parallel to uuu. Opposite edges of a rhombus cancel in the oriented boundary sum. Internal edges cancel between adjacent tiles. Consequently, the boundary contains equal numbers of +u+u+u- and −u-u−u-oriented unit edges.

By convexity, edges having a given orientation occupy a single straight boundary chain. Therefore the uuu-edges occur on two opposite parallel boundary sides, and every uuu-track connects these sides.

For another direction v≠uv\ne uv=u modulo π\piπ, the four relevant boundary sides occur in alternating cyclic order:

u+,v+,u−,v−,u_+,\quad v_+,\quad u_-,\quad v_-,u+​,v+​,u−​,v−​,

up to reversal and cyclic permutation. This follows because the oriented tangent direction of a convex polygon advances monotonically through a complete turn.

Choose any uuu-track and any vvv-track. Their boundary endpoints alternate. Two arcs in a disk whose endpoints alternate on the boundary must intersect, by the Jordan separation principle.

Represent tracks inside each rhombus by segments joining midpoints of opposite edges. An intersection between tracks of distinct directions occurs inside a rhombus crossed by both tracks. That rhombus has edge directions uuu and vvv.

Hence every pair of distinct edge directions occurs together in at least one rhombus. □\square□

The proof survives boundary vertices that are collinear along a side. They merely subdivide a parallelogram side into unit segments. The grid count uses all such vertices, not merely the extreme points of the convex hull.

### Connelly: universal rigidity from PSD stress

Robert Connelly, Tensegrities and Global Rigidity (2009), Theorem 5, p. 14.

Primary text: [Cornell PDF](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~connelly/Tensegrity-Global.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com). pi.math.cornell.edu

Its hypotheses are:

1. The configuration affinely spans Rd\mathbb R^dRd, with a proper equilibrium stress.
2. Its stress matrix is PSD.
3. Its rank is n−d−1n-d-1n−d−1.
4. Its stressed directions do not lie on a quadric at infinity.

The conclusion is universal global rigidity: every realization satisfying the same unilateral constraints, in any Euclidean dimension, is congruent.

Connelly's earlier Stress and Stability, Theorem 2.6, p. 25, includes the additional hypothesis that every vertex belongs to a nonzero-stress member.

Primary text: [Cornell chapter PDF](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~connelly/Tensegrity.Chapter.2.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com). pi.math.cornell.edu

Applicability: Both are sufficient theorems. The negative-trace identity rules out their PSD hypothesis for the present physical stresses. Failure of that hypothesis does not imply flexibility.

### Connelly: the convex-polygon PSD theorem

Robert Connelly, Rigidity and Energy, Inventiones Mathematicae 66 (1982), 11–33.

Primary text: [Original article PDF](https://connellytensegrity.com/pdf/10.1007_BF01404753.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

Relevant results:

- Theorem 5, p. 26: for vertices forming a convex polygon, with cables on its boundary, struts inside, and a nonzero proper stress, the stress matrix is PSD with nullity three.
- Corollary 1, p. 27: the corresponding framework is uniquely embedded, even in higher dimensions.
- Theorem 3, p. 16: rigidity of a framework containing a cable or strut implies existence of a nonzero proper stress. The converse is not asserted. connellytensegrity.com

Applicability: The theorem has exactly the opposite geometric placement from the proposed framework. Its cables surround the polygon; its struts connect polygon vertices internally.

Here, diameter cables join selected exposed leaves, while positive unit struts form a tree with internal vertices. The boundary-cable hypothesis fails, and the negative-trace identity independently excludes the conclusion.

B. Roth and W. Whiteley, Tensegrity Frameworks, Transactions of the AMS 265 (1981), 419–446.

Original article: [Author-hosted copy of the journal PDF](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Walter-Whiteley/publication/243079162_Tensegrity_Frameworks/links/0f31753b4a8ee0a3c0000000/Tensegrity-Frameworks.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

Theorem 5.2, p. 427: a tensegrity is infinitesimally rigid if and only if its underlying bar framework is infinitesimally rigid and it has a proper stress, with strictly appropriate signs on every cable and strut. The theorem also gives equivalent formulations involving regular placements. Roth–Whiteley use the opposite stress-sign convention from Connelly's later papers. ResearchGate

Applicability: Equilibrium alone is insufficient. The underlying framework must also pass a rigidity-rank test, and a physical certificate containing zero-weight full constraints need not furnish the strictly proper stress required for the entire full graph.
